title: Instagram
summary: Build a photo and video sharing service with fast media delivery and a hybrid home feed.
narrative:
A photo upload should appear in followers' home feeds without slowing down a scrolling session. Build Instagram for ~500 M daily active users: upload photos and videos, follow users, and fetch a cursor-paginated feed of followed accounts. At ~100 M uploads/day and an average photo size of ~2 MB, originals alone add ~200 TB/day before replication and derived variants. Reads dominate, and a home feed should load in under 200 ms.

Keep original media and resized thumbnail, feed and full-size variants in Blob Storage, while a NoSQL Database stores post IDs, authors, timestamps and media pointers. Clients fetch media through the CDN and send API requests through a Load Balancer to redundant Web Servers. This design proxies original uploads through the app tier and delivers images through the CDN. Presigned direct-to-storage uploads are also a valid architecture, outside this chosen topology. The UI loads appropriately sized images, lazy-loads below the fold and prefetches the next page.

After accepting an upload, publish a new-post event to a Message Queue. Redundant Workers generate media variants and fan out ordinary authors' post IDs into cached follower feeds; retries must not duplicate entries. Celebrity posts are not pushed to millions of feeds: merge their recent posts from the post store at read time. A Graph Database can supply follower lookups, and Monitoring can track processing lag and delivery failures.

functional: Upload photos and videos; follow users and scroll a cursor-paginated home feed
Store originals and resized variants in Blob Storage; keep post metadata and media pointers in NoSQL
Serve thumbnail, feed and full-size variants through the CDN; lazy-load and prefetch images in the UI
Queue new-post events for Workers to resize media and update cached follower feeds
Push ordinary posts into feeds; merge celebrity posts from the post store at read time
nonFunctional: Load the home feed in under 200 ms
Scale a heavily read-dominant workload and keep media durable
Continue API service and background processing after a single instance failure
constraints: Route API requests through the Load Balancer and Web Server tier
Proxy uploads through the app in this design and deliver media through the CDN; presigned direct uploads are an alternative outside this topology
Access post metadata through the Web Server tier; deduplicate retried feed updates
capacity: ~500 M DAU; ~100 M uploads/day ≈ 1,160 uploads/s on average
~2 MB average photo → ~200 TB/day of originals before replication and resized variants
specs.tradeoff: Precomputed feeds make reads cheap but amplify writes; merging celebrity posts on read avoids enormous fan-out. Resized CDN variants use extra storage to reduce bandwidth and image load time.
specs.bonus: Connect Workers to a Graph Database for follower lookup and add Monitoring for feed and media processing.

topologyRules.message: Images reach users through the CDN; this design routes uploads through the app tier.
API requests must enter through the Load Balancer.
Post metadata access must pass through the Web Server tier.

resilienceRules.message: Run at least two Web Servers to keep uploads and feeds available during an instance failure.
Run at least two Workers so media processing and fan-out survive an instance failure.
Connect Blob Storage to the CDN for efficient media delivery.

hints: Separate media bytes from post metadata: use Client → CDN → Blob Storage for delivery and Client → Load Balancer → Web Server for API calls. Store originals through Web Server → Blob Storage and metadata through Web Server → NoSQL.

Connect Web Server → Cache for feeds and Web Server → Message Queue → Worker for new posts. Connect Worker → Blob Storage for resized variants and → Cache for ordinary-author fan-out; merge celebrity posts from NoSQL at read time.

Run two Web Servers and two Workers, wiring each replica to the same dependencies. Connect Workers to a Graph Database for follower lookup and Web Servers to Monitoring. Keep all client metadata access behind the app and image delivery through the CDN.
